requirement:
When Habeas loads legacy evidence with an unknown criterion version, the SDK
record holds `None`. In-place conversion writes `"*"` in `review_version` so
the converted file preserves that history. An unknown version passes the
version check under
{cite}`requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.checking_records.version_match`.
The record is current when its recorded inputs and all existing application
freshness checks still match. Version matching leaves the subject, reference-set,
input, determination, citation, and site checks intact.

For new assessments, Habeas Codicem's validation value supplies a concrete review version
other than `*`, and the assessment records it.
rationale:
The reviewed tests cover each obligation in `requirements.sdk.habeas.evidence_conversion.legacy_freshness`. I judged this from the supplied test source and did not read any implementation source.

- **Legacy evidence with an unknown version loads as `None`.**
  - `src/evidence_format.rs#mod[tests]/fn[legacy_conversion_preserves_every_historical_field_without_resolving_sources]` decodes legacy requirement, example, citation and site records and asserts `record.version == None`.
  - `src/authoring/sdk.rs#mod[tests]/fn[every_review_kind_loads_both_formats_and_reports_each_application_failure_once]` loads legacy files through `load_evidence` for all four review kinds and asserts `loaded.version == None`.
- **In-place conversion writes `"*"` and preserves history.**
  - `src/authoring/sdk.rs#mod[tests]/fn[current_legacy_authoring_converts_without_configuration_and_stdout_never_converts]` converts a legacy file in place. It asserts `review_version == "*"` and that `view(new) == old`.
  - The `evidence_format` test above asserts the same for every subject kind: the encoded `review_version` is `"*"` and `view(native) == old`.
- **An unknown version passes the version check, and a known version must match.**
  - `native_freshness_checks_versions_inputs_and_application_fields` shows a `None` version is current against `future-review-version`.
  - The same test shows a saved concrete `old-concrete-version` is not current against `review_version()`. This is the contrast with the cited `version_match` behavior.
- **A record is current when its inputs and all application checks match.**
  - The multi-kind authoring test asserts there are no findings for the legacy file. It asserts the same for native files with `"*"` and with the concrete version, and the loaded dependencies and output equal the decoded ones.
- **Version matching leaves the subject, reference-set, input, determination, citation and site checks intact.**
  - That test applies per-kind mutations to `"*"`-versioned records and asserts a finding in each case. The legacy and converted native files give identical findings, and `load_evidence` still returns `Some`, so staleness is an application finding rather than a loading error.
  - Every kind gets a false determination and a changed input. Definitions also get changed text and a changed reference set. Citations get changed `file`, `item` and commentary. Sites get changed `requirement`, `file`, `item`, `queries`, `fixmes`, and `applies:false`.
  - `native_freshness_checks_versions_inputs_and_application_fields` also shows that a changed subject text makes a `None`-version record not current.
- **New assessments record a concrete review version other than `*`.**
  - `authoring_keeps_the_prepared_subject_snapshot_and_concrete_version` asserts `value["review_version"] == REVIEW_VERSION` and `!= "*"`.
  - The same test decodes the new record and asserts it is not current once the subject text has changed.

All of these tests carry a `{test}` reference to the subject. I found no unexercised obligation or boundary case that the text names.
